I know this is a minority opinion, especially here, but I don't view the ISDS component of the TPP in such a negative light. It's being forced into a narrative of narrow government oppression, but imo is something more akin to parties agreeing they are on amiable enough terms to agree to arbitration to solve their problems rather than full legal proceedings. ISDS is evidence that we are of like enough mind with our trade partners to agree to a common and, at least relatively, efficient process of solving differences that may occur.

Keep in mind that this kind of provision can also be used to challenge countries engaging in a race to the bottom as well. If a country is allowing child labor, excessive hours, or extreme underpayment, then theoretically a party could challenge those practices under the ISDS as well. ISDS' existence in and of itself is not necessarily a negative thing.

Additionally, a party could always simply choose to leave the TPP if they felt their sovereignty was sufficiently impaired beyond their marginal benefit. Imo, the TPP is likely to be successful in standardizing labor differences in the US/Aus/JPN/NZ with the industrial powers in SE Asia/S. America. I think it's likely India and China will sign on once they see implementation in the existing negotiating parties, the value of which is, at least in my opinion, obvious.

Or, a company like Monsanto could sue the subscribing EU nations for forcing the labeling of GMO's because it hurts their business. This is absolute crap because it puts business interests in front of every other issue, environmental, public health, or otherwise. Of course, we already knew that. That's why it's secret.

I think we're being presumptive to assume one way or the other on the outcome of ISDS cases. However, I also question what sort of enforcement mechanisms would even be in place to support ISDS outcomes. For example, even if a company were to obtain an ISDS judgment in their favor, what would that mean for the counterparty? Is there some sort of TPP removal mechanism? In that situation then, you've gotten the outcome you already wanted from the start, which is no TPP in place.

The negotiations being held in secret isn't really a negative to me either. We'll be able to see the finished the product and discuss it then. Negotiations with other countries have always been the executive's power rather than the legislative's because of the mess it would be to subject ongoing negotiations to wavering public opinion and, in my opinion, generally ignorant/naive viewpoints (of which I acknowledge my own are generally part of, as IANAL).
